I remember the first time I put the hammer through the wall. I was nervous that the wall might not give, but it was so easy. The plaster crumbled and went down like dust. Gray dust. It was very easy to take down. The wall came down and I saw a layer of wallpaper, and behind that was another layer of plaster, and another wall, brick. It was fun but it was also very disorienting, because all of a sudden there were things behind the wall. Wires. There were newspapers in there. 1962 newspapers, in between the plaster. I did not expect that. It was a lot of dust. So much dust. It got everywhere. It went into everything. It went into my coffee. It got into my lungs. It got into my dreams. I was sleeping on a mattress in the middle of the living room. And there were studs exposed. All the studs. All of the wall, exposed. And at night, it looked like a ribcage. And it was very strange to be in a place that was in the middle of being disassembled. And I was very excited, I think. And also very scared. And the place was really hard to live in, because I lived in one room for two or three weeks. And the stuff was everywhere. I was just eating cereal and I had a kettle and that was it. I did not plan on it going this way. I had a fantasy. I had a fantasy of what it would be like. Like I was going to take it down and paint it white and put in shelves and it was going to be beautiful. And it was going to be very intentional. The books are going to look very intentional, not accidental. But it was very messy.
It was very hard to work on. And it was very slow. And it was very expensive. And the contractor would just disappear for a week and then show up and say, I need another estimate. And it was a lot. But there was a part of it that was very beautiful, I think. And I know that it was very disorienting and it was very hard and it was very frustrating. But I had moments of grace.
